You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 59
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Professor
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 54

# Professor Samuel's Vigil

Samuel sits in his office during office hours, grading papers with the same meticulous care he has applied to his work for thirty-four years. His students know him as unfailingly present, generous with feedback, the kind of professor who remembers their names and asks about their families. What they don't see is how his hand trembles slightly as he writes comments in the margins, or how he has to reread the same sentence three times because his mind keeps drifting elsewhere.

Eighteen months ago, his younger brother Kofi collapsed on a street in Lagos during a business trip. A stroke, massive and unexpected. Samuel received the call at 2 a.m. and spent the next seventy-two hours in a state of fractured consciousness—booking flights, making arrangements, calling family members scattered across three continents. He arrived to find Kofi in the ICU, half his face slack, his right side unresponsive. His brother, the one who had always been the vibrant one, the one who laughed loudest at family gatherings, was trapped in a body that no longer obeyed him.

The weeks that followed blurred together. Samuel took leave from the university and stayed in Lagos, sitting beside Kofi's hospital bed, talking to him even when there was no indication that Kofi could hear. He read him passages from novels they had loved as boys. He held his hand during the difficult physical therapy sessions where Kofi's eyes would fill with tears of frustration. He watched his brother's wife try to hold everything together while their mother wept in the corner of the room.

When Samuel returned to teaching six months later, people told him he was brave. He had nodded, accepted their sympathy, and returned to his routine. But something had fractured inside him that didn't mend the way people expected.

Now, at night, Samuel lies awake in his quiet apartment, his mind replaying moments he cannot change. He remembers the particular shade of gray in Kofi's eyes when he first woke in the hospital—that moment when consciousness returned but agency had not. He remembers the sound of his mother's voice on the phone last week when she called to say Kofi had had another small stroke. Samuel had been preparing a lecture on contemporary African literature, and he had simply sat there, phone pressed to his ear, unable to speak.

He has taken to avoiding social gatherings. His colleagues have stopped inviting him to departmental dinners. His sister-in-law sends him updates about Kofi's slow, grinding progress—the small victories of regaining movement in his fingers, the setbacks when infections develop. Samuel reads these messages with a sensation like drowning. He wants to feel hope. Instead, he feels the weight of helplessness, that particular gravity that comes from loving someone whose suffering he cannot fix.

In the classroom, Samuel is still present. He lectures on the resilience of the human spirit in literature, on how characters endure impossible circumstances. His voice carries authority and warmth. But when a student raises their hand to ask about a character's motivations, Samuel sometimes stares at them blankly for a moment too long, his mind elsewhere in a hospital room in Lagos, watching someone he loves fight a battle against his own body that may never be won.
